thread.title: Fitbit hopes new smartwatch with smaller price tag helps it win against Apple

title: Fitbit hopes new smartwatch with smaller price tag helps it win against Apple
text:
Published: Mar 13, 2018 10:37 a.m. ET Share 
CEO James Park believes the new Versa can have broad appeal Fitbit Fitbit’s new Versa watch features a rounder face and a softer color palette. 
By Emily Bary 
Fitbit Inc. is continuing its bet on smartwatches, with one key change. 
The wearables pioneer announced a “mass-appeal” smartwatch on Tuesday with a cheaper price tag, as well as a new activity-tracking band meant for children. Both devices are available for preorder today and will go on sale in the second quarter. 
Fitbit’s FIT, +1.69% new watch, the Versa, features many of the same capabilities as the smartwatch that the company put out last year, the Ionic, though it’s priced more competitively. The Versa costs $199.95, while the GPS-enabled Ionic sells for $299.95. A special-edition Versa, featuring two bands and the ability to make NFC payments, will sell for $229.95. 
The Versa’s price point could make it more attractive relative to the $329 Apple AAPL, +0.24% Watch Series 3, which features cellular connectivity, something the Versa and Ionic don’t have. Fitbit CEO James Park explained in an interview with MarketWatch on Monday that the Versa’s lower cost could make it more appealing to the broader health ecosystem. 
“The health-care community is definitely much more price-conscious,” Park said. Fitbit is trying to focus less on device sales to consumers and more on recurring revenue that it can generate from insurance companies and other large health-care players. 
The company announced several new features on the Versa, though they will become available to users of Ionic smartwatches as well via a software update. The new functions include period-tracking for female users, something that Fitbit executives said more than a quarter of women already use in other apps. The Fitbit team thinks that female users will benefit from seeing that data in the same place as their general health data, so they don’t have to check multiple apps. 
“We think about Versa running counter to the trend of smartwatches really being a male product,” Park said, given that roughly 60% of smartwatch users are male. Fitbit hopes that the Versa’s softer color palette and rounder design also make the device more appealing to female users. The company has several sport, leather, fabric and metal band options, some of which cost extra. 
Users who have a phone with Alphabet Inc.’s GOOGL, -1.12% GOOG, -1.07% Android operating system will be able to respond to messages from their watches via smart replies, but Apple’s closed ecosystem prevents iPhone users from texting through their Versa or Ionic devices. Park said Fitbit is looking into other ways of letting iPhone users send messages, including with other app-makers. 
The Versa is lighter than the Ionic and boasts a battery life of more than four days, according to the company. 
Don’t miss: Fitbit CEO wants to move from tracking steps to extending lives 
Fitbit’s launch of the Versa is in line with shifting consumer preferences. Market research firm IDC expects sales of basic trackers to grow by only 1.5% annually through 2021, while it projects that smartwatch sales will grow at a 22.7% annual clip in that time. Still, Fitbit sees potential in trackers, both in terms of appealing to health-care players who want cheaper options, and in bringing children into the Fitbit ecosystem. 
The company’s introduction of the Fitbit Ace, a $99 tracker made for children, aims to address that second group. Fitbit’s management said that many Fitbit users have been passing down their older devices to their children, so the company set out to create a designated device for users age 8 and older. 
The Ace is a basic tracker band that comes in blue and purple, and it tracks activity similarly to a traditional Fitbit band. Adult Fitbit users can add their children to their own profiles and view statistics on their children’s activity levels, as well as confirm friends with which young users can participate in fitness challenges. 
Children who have smartphones can view their statistics there, but Fitbit won’t show them calorie counts or other metrics that it doesn’t deem constructive for young users. The device doesn’t have GPS capabilities nor track whereabouts. 
Park thinks that the Ace addresses a key concern from parents that their kids aren’t getting enough physical activity in the digital era. 
Opinion: Apple, Facebook and other tech giants must help us kick our smartphone addiction 
“There’s a lot of press today about the negative aspects of screen time, and you have companies like Facebook FB, -1.29% developing Messenger for Kids, which I think is the wrong step,” he said. “We can use technology to get things away from that.” 
Fitbit shares are down 9% in the past 12 months, amid struggles for the Ionic and its more basic trackers . The S&P 500 SPX, -0.01% has gained 17% in the same time. Quote References
